items.title: 0.9999... equals 1, exactly
items.claim: The decimal expansion 0.999... (infinitely many 9s) does not approach 1 — it IS 1. Two different decimal expansions can represent the same real number.

options.text: They're approximately equal but slightly different
They have zero difference (1 - 0.999... = 0); 0.999... = sum of 9/10 to the n for n from 1 to infinity = 9/10 / (1 - 1/10) = 1 exactly

items.reveal:
Every infinite decimal expansion is, by definition, a convergent series.
0.999... = 9/10 + 9/100 + 9/1000 + ...
     = 9/10 * (1 + 1/10 + 1/100 + ...)
     = 9/10 * 1/(1 - 1/10)
     = 9/10 * 10/9
     = 1

Another argument: let x = 0.999... Then 10x = 9.999... Subtract: 10x - x = 9.999... - 0.999... so 9x = 9 and x = 1.

Third argument: the difference 1 - 0.999... is less than 10 to the minus n for every n. The only non-negative real with this property is 0. So 1 - 0.999... = 0 and 0.999... = 1.

Decimals are a representation, not an identity. Any real with a terminating decimal also has a 999...-style alternative: 0.5 = 0.4999..., 1 = 0.999..., 0.123 = 0.122999... The two representations are equal.

In educational settings this is one of the most strongly contested results — students often refuse to accept it. The objection is usually based on confusing representations with the numbers themselves.
items.why: Decimals feel like unique addresses for numbers. They are not — every terminating decimal has a recurring-9 twin, and equality of the two is logically forced.

items.title: A 1-in-300-million lottery ticket is almost always a bad investment
items.claim: Mega Millions: ~302 million possible combinations. A ticket costs $2. Jackpot of $600 million sounds like positive expected value (EV = 600M/302M = $2 — break even). But after taxes, lump sum discount, and ticket-splitting, real EV is well below $2.
items.prompt: How do you compute expected value correctly?

options.text: Sum over all outcomes of (probability * value). For a fair calculation, include ALL outcomes (not just the jackpot), tax adjustments, and the fact that big jackpots often have multiple winners who split the prize
Expected value is just the prize size

items.reveal:
Naive EV calculation for a lottery:
- Prize: $600M.
- Win probability: 1 / 302,000,000.
- EV from jackpot only: $600M / 302M ≈ $1.99.
- Ticket cost: $2.
- Naive net: -$0.01.

Real adjustments:
- Federal tax (~37% top bracket) plus state tax (variable, say 5%): take-home ~$330M instead of $600M.
- Lump sum vs annuity: lump sum is ~60% of advertised jackpot. Pre-tax lump sum: ~$360M. Post-tax: ~$200M.
- Jackpot splitting: when jackpots get large, more people play. Probability of multiple winners rises. Expected share is less than full jackpot.
- Other prizes: smaller wins (matching some numbers) contribute roughly $0.30 of EV per ticket. Better, but not enough.

Realistic EV: usually $0.50 - $1.00 per $2 ticket. Lottery is a regressive tax on the mathematically uninformed.

Linearity of expectation: E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y], even if X and Y aren't independent. A surprisingly powerful tool. The St. Petersburg paradox (already covered) is an exception where naive EV is infinite but psychological/practical value is finite.

Kelly criterion: optimal bet sizing when you have an edge. Even with positive EV, betting too much can lead to ruin. Bet fraction equals edge / odds. Most gamblers overbet, even when statistically lucky.

Applications:
- Insurance: companies sell policies with positive EV (for them); buyers accept negative EV in exchange for risk reduction.
- Investment decisions: long-run wealth is dominated by GEOMETRIC mean returns (Kelly).
- Game theory: mixed-strategy equilibria depend on equalising opponents' expected payoffs.
items.why: Expected value seems intuitive. Real computations require including hidden costs, taxes, and the structure of outcomes. The lottery survives because most players don't actually compute the math correctly — and because the entertainment value is real.

items.title: Achilles can never catch the tortoise
items.claim: Zeno's paradox: Achilles gives the tortoise a head start. To catch it, he must reach where the tortoise was — by then the tortoise has moved a bit. Repeat infinitely. He performs infinitely many tasks and can never reach the tortoise.

options.text: Achilles is actually slower than the tortoise
Infinitely many finite tasks can take finite total time — the geometric series 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... sums to 1, not infinity

items.reveal_title: Zeno's paradoxes and the calculus that resolves them
items.reveal:
Zeno of Elea (c. 490-430 BC) offered several paradoxes about motion:
- Dichotomy: to walk across a room, you must first walk half-way, then half of what remains, etc. Infinite steps.
- Achilles and the tortoise: as above.
- Arrow: at each instant, an arrow occupies a fixed position, so it isn't moving — yet motion sums to a journey.

Resolution requires the concept of convergent infinite series — formalised in the 17th and 19th centuries by Newton, Leibniz, Cauchy and Weierstrass. The sum 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... equals 2, not infinity. Infinitely many tasks can be completed in finite time, provided their durations form a convergent series.

The paradoxes pre-dated rigorous calculus by 2000 years. Zeno's challenge actually pushed mathematicians toward developing the tools needed to handle infinity and the continuum properly. Mathematicians sometimes joke that Zeno was the first calculus student to fail to grasp limits.
items.why: Common sense rules out infinite tasks in finite time. Mathematical analysis shows infinite tasks of decreasing size can totalise to finite quantities — and motion proceeds.
